source: Mirzaei (2026) Sample More, Reflect Less: Self-Refine and Reflexion Lose to Repeated Sampling at Equal Token Cost, 1.5B to 7B
finding: Designed re-test of Wang et al.'s claim that self-consistency beats reasoning strategies at equal compute. Seven methods, Qwen2.5 1.5B/3B/7B, two math sets, every token counted, paired bootstrap with Holm correction. No method beats repeated sampling at its own measured cost. All 18 comparisons that involve self-inspection are negative.
numbers: 150 questions per benchmark (GSM8K, MATH-500); 36 paired comparisons; 10 reliably worse than cost-matched sampling, 2 survive the all-36 correction; none favours the method.
quote: Self-Refine and Reflexion lose to repeated sampling at equal token cost
limits: Single author, small question sets, Qwen2.5 only, 7B top size, no learned trigger tested (prompted methods only). So it does not test ReVISE, but it is the nearest equal-token check we found.
agent_relevance: Any S5 review pass must be compared with extra sampled votes at equal tokens. Prompted self-inspection loses at every size up to 7B.

source: Mirzaei (2026) Sample More, Reflect Less - rewrite versus choose
finding: Rewriting does not recover with scale. Self-Refine and a forced Reflexion stay significantly below the cost-matched baseline at 7B. Reflexion run as published never triggered its own retry on the 1.5B model: it called itself correct on every question and so collapsed into one cheap chain of thought.
numbers: At 7B: Reflexion (forced) -5.5 pp GSM8K CI [-10.2,-1.2] and -10.1 pp MATH-500 CI [-15.0,-5.7]; Self-Refine -3.6 pp GSM8K CI [-6.9,-0.9] and -6.3 pp MATH-500 CI [-11.1,-2.0]. 1.5B MATH-500: Self-Refine 47.3 vs 52.3 cost-matched baseline.
quote: A method that decides for itself when to act can stop acting without any outward sign
limits: Reflexion trigger failure is prompt-specific by the author's own note. Row-to-method alignment in the PDF table text is garbled; figures here are the ones stated in the prose.
agent_relevance: A self-judged trigger can silently go to 'never refine'. Log the trigger rate in every run; a trigger firing 0% of the time looks like a cheap success.

source: Mirzaei (2026) Sample More, Reflect Less - Best-of-N by self-choice versus counting
finding: Same eight samples, only the last step differs: the model picks the best, or we count the most common answer. Counting wins at small size and the gap vanishes at 7B. So model self-choice is the weak step, and it improves with size.
numbers: Counting beats model-chosen by 8.0 and 11.3 points at 1.5B (two benchmarks) but only 2.0 and 1.3 points at 7B, not distinguishable from zero. At 1.5B and 3B counting wins by 5 to 17 points.
quote: choosing is worse than counting below 7B, and the two draw level at 7B
limits: Only Qwen2.5 up to 7B; says nothing about 70B or frontier models.
agent_relevance: Prefer vote/agreement as the S5 signal over asking a small model to judge. Own-judgement may become acceptable only at larger scale.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Mid-trace shifts ('Wait, actually') in RL-tuned models are rare and go with LOWER accuracy, not higher. They look like instability, not a self-correction mechanism.
numbers: Qwen2.5-1.5B GRPO runs, N=723,200 traces over crossword, math and Rush Hour: shifts in about 7.6% of samples (6.31% pooled over models), accuracy 2.57% with a shift vs 16.44% without. 1M+ traces in the whole study. External check on MATH-500: DeepSeek-R1 shifts 0.00 to 0.25%, GPT-4o 0.88 to 2.21%, no consistent accuracy gain.
quote: reasoning shifts are rare, do not become more frequent with training, and seldom improve accuracy
limits: Shifts found by lexical cues plus a plan-change detector, so unwritten shifts are missed. Mostly a 1.5B model; R1 shift counts are tiny so its estimates are unstable.
agent_relevance: Do not trust spontaneous 'wait' behaviour as a free S5 trigger. Spontaneous re-entry is a symptom of trouble, not a repair.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight - forced reconsideration cue under high entropy
finding: Appending a fixed reconsideration cue ('Wait, we need to reconsider. Let's think this through step by step.') and re-querying gave large paired gains on math, and gains were larger on the high-entropy fifth of questions. This is a no-training, entropy-gated re-entry.
numbers: Math: N=320,000 paired samples, Pass-1 0.3221 to Pass-2 0.4062 (+8.41 pp); wrong-to-right 50,574 vs right-to-wrong 23,500. Crossword +0.45 pp (5,380 vs 5,004). Rush Hour +0.01 pp (near-zero base). Gate: top 20% pass-1 sequence entropy.
quote: artificially triggering extrinsic shifts under high entropy reliably improves accuracy
limits: Pass 2 is a second full generation with a cue; there is NO equal-token resample control, so part of the gain may be plain resampling. Baseline accuracy low (0.32) so headroom is large. Right-to-wrong is not small (23,500 flips): net positive, but the cost is real. Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama only.
agent_relevance: Closest published test of a prompted, entropy-gated Wait re-entry with measured right-to-wrong cost. Needs the same-token resample control before we adopt it.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight - stratified by entropy
finding: Even among high-entropy traces, spontaneous shifts in math remain harmful. In the low-entropy majority they are much worse. So entropy marks where a forced re-check pays, not where the model's own re-check works.
numbers: Math raw accuracy gap for a shift: -7.40 pp in the top-20% entropy stratum, -22.88 pp in the bottom 80%. Crossword high-entropy stratum +0.63 pp (noisy).
quote: High entropy does not cause more spontaneous pivots
limits: Observational (shifts are not randomised); problem fixed effects used but confounding with difficulty remains.
agent_relevance: Use entropy or logprob as the gate for S5; do not wait for the model to decide to re-check by itself.

source: Del, Kangsepp, Domnich, Tampuu, Yankovskaya, Kull, Fishel (2026) How Uncertainty Estimation Scales with Sampling in Reasoning Models
finding: No-training confidence signals from reasoning models are already decent from one sample. A single verbalized-confidence read gives AUROC in the 70s on math; self-consistency with 2 samples is lower than verbalized confidence, and does not overtake it up to 8 samples.
numbers: 17 tasks, 3 reasoning models, several sampling budgets K. VC at K=1: 78.8 AUROC MMLU-Pro Math, 68.7 GSM8K, 66.4 AIME, 73.8 STEM average, 68.5 humanities. Math K=2: SC 70.5 vs VC 73.5. VC rises by up to +10.1 AUROC from K=1 to K=8 in math. Model names taken from footnote links (gpt-oss-20b, Qwen3-30B-A3B, R1-0528-Qwen3-8B).
quote: self-consistency exhibits lower initial discrimination and lags behind verbalized confidence under moderate sampling
limits: Predicts correctness of the final answer, not whether a refine would fix it. Confidence prompts matter a lot (AIME VC was prompt-sensitive). Reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: A no-training P(correct) read-out reaches the same range as ReVISE's AUROC (76.0) on math. Gap 3 is largely answered yes for math with reasoning models.

source: Del et al. (2026) How Uncertainty Estimation Scales with Sampling - hybrid signal
finding: Mixing verbalized confidence and self-consistency beats either alone, even when either is given 4x more samples. Gains are biggest in math.
numbers: Two-sample hybrid (SCVC) +12.9 AUROC in math and +6.4 in STEM and humanities over one-sample VC; beats VC or SC at K=8 in all domains. Math: +2.7 more from K=2 to 5 and +1.5 from 5 to 8; STEM/humanities about +1 to +2 beyond K=2. Domain-averaged AUROC of six elicitation variants about 67.6 to 77.0 (Table 3).
quote: with just two samples, a hybrid estimator improves AUROC by up to +12 on average
limits: AUROC says nothing about calibration of the threshold we would choose. Cost: each extra sample is a full chain.
agent_relevance: A cheap S5 trigger: one verbalized-confidence read plus answer agreement across 2 samples. Test this against ReVISE-style numbers.

source: Kang, Deng, Xiao, Mo, Lee, Bing (2025) First Try Matters: Revisiting the Role of Reflection in Reasoning Models
finding: In long-CoT reasoning models, most reflection after the first candidate answer just confirms it. Corrective reflections (wrong to right) are rare, so the first try decides the result. Reflection eats a big share of tokens for a small gain.
numbers: 8 reasoning models, 5 math benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH500). Over 90% of reflections confirm (right-right or wrong-wrong same); wrong-to-right mostly under 2%. Reflection after the first candidate uses 16.8 to 47.8% of tokens and adds 1.4 to 3.5 points. Truncating reflection once a candidate appears saves 24.5% tokens for under 2.9% accuracy loss.
quote: reflections are predominantly confirmatory and rarely alter the model's initial answer
limits: Pre-trained reasoning models, observational counts of answer changes. Right-to-wrong counts are not in the headline numbers I read.
agent_relevance: On R1-style models the extra refine pass is mostly redundant (gap 6): a fixed or learned stop-after-first-answer is the cheaper lever. Reflection was more frequent on easy problems, so it is not aligned with difficulty.

source: Rakasi, Lalwani, Srivastava, Palanivel, Adeleke, Li, Wu (2026) When Uncertainty Isn't Enough: Self-Correction in Code Generation
finding: Cheap uncertainty signals do not predict code correctness well enough to drive self-correction. Only multi-sample P(True) correlated strongly, and only on two of three small models. Acting on the weak signals made greedy outputs worse.
numbers: HumanEval, 3 small code LLMs (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B). Correlation with pass/fail: P(True) 0.842, 0.782, 0.303; mean token entropy -0.416, -0.234, -0.216; verbalized -0.327, -0.090, -0.114. Uncertainty-triggered regeneration lowered Pass@1 in all three HumanEval configs (-3.23 to -9.68 pp); on BigCodeBench 2 of 3 worse (-3.23, -3.87; DeepSeek +5.81).
quote: uncertainty-based self-correction fails to reliably improve Pass@1, degrading accuracy in 5 of 6 configurations
limits: HumanEval held-out n=31 only; BigCodeBench n=155; small 1B-3B models; workshop paper. Correlations are Pearson with pass/fail.
agent_relevance: Boundary for gap 3: no-training logprob/entropy triggers can fail on code; the one that works costs several samples. Do not assume math AUROC carries to code.

source: Rakasi et al. (2026) When Uncertainty Isn't Enough - verification-based correction
finding: The only policy that reliably improved Pass@1 was verification-based correction, and gains were larger when the base model was weaker. It cost several times the latency of greedy decoding.
numbers: HumanEval gains +6 to +26 pp (DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B 0.61 to 0.87, +25.81 pp at 2.4x latency); BigCodeBench +7.74 to +20.00 pp (Llama 0.271 to 0.368 at 5.9x latency; Qwen 0.297 to 0.374 at 5.0x; DeepSeek 0.181 to 0.381 at 5.0x).
quote: Only verification-based self-correction reliably improves Pass@1
limits: Paper text calls these the 'costlier execution-based correction loops'; I did not confirm exactly what the verifier runs. Latency cost, not matched-token; no best-of-N comparison at equal cost.
agent_relevance: Where a checker exists (code), checker-driven S5 beats uncertainty-driven S5 in accuracy but costs 2.4x to 5.9x time. Gap 5 partly closed for code; no evidence here for tasks with no checker.

source: Xiong, Zhang, Ye, Chen, Jiang, Zhang (2025) Self-rewarding correction for mathematical reasoning
finding: An independent group trained a model to write its own correct/incorrect verdict after a first answer and revise only on 'incorrect'. Qwen2.5-Math-7B (and Llama-3) gain over single-turn baselines by a few points. Prompted intrinsic self-correction reduced accuracy because the model edits regardless of correctness.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-base, greedy. Self-rewarding IFT + DPO: MATH500 78.6, OlympiadBench 40.1, Minerva 34.6 vs single-turn DPO 76.8, 39.0, 31.6 (about +1.8, +1.1, +3.0). Self-verdict accuracy, DPO iter 5, MATH500: recognises correct 92.0%, recognises wrong 50.6% (PPO step 220: 98.6% / 47.6%).
quote: intrinsic self-correction without explicit reward signals typically reduces final test accuracy
limits: Gold-correctness reward used in training; Qwen2.5-Math is math-specialised; paper says self-rewarding models use more inference tokens (I did not extract the number) and has no equal-token best-of-N control. The results table in the PDF text is column-garbled, so gains are from the prose.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1 in part: a second group, Qwen and Llama, reproduces the 1 to 3 point gain pattern. Also gives a usable operating point: about 50% recall on wrong, about 8% false alarm on right.

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE - Table 4 transfer MATH to GSM8K (re-read for gap 7)
finding: Trained on MATH, tested on GSM8K, ReVISE keeps a small edge over baselines. The edge is about half a point at 1B and about one point at 8B, smaller than in-domain.
numbers: Llama-3.2-1B: SFT 7.3, RFT 8.2, STaR+ 8.0, ReVISE 8.8. Llama-3.1-8B: SFT 60.3, RFT 60.3, STaR+ 58.7, ReVISE 61.5. No AIME or GPQA tested.
quote: both model sizes significantly outperform other baselines in this out-of-distribution evaluation
limits: No variance reported; gains of 0.6 and 1.2 points are within what a different seed could move. Only Llama; only math to math.
agent_relevance: Trigger transfer is untested for harder or non-math sets; assume the trigger needs recalibration per task.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench - natural errors and the Wait cue (re-read for gap 4)
finding: Across 14 non-reasoning models the blind spot averages 64.5%: models fix an error placed in the user turn but not the same error in their own turn. Appending 'Wait' cuts the blind spot by 89.3% with no training. The paper also tests natural own-generated errors, but only in part.
numbers: SFT on 5,306 correction traces cuts the blind spot 76.0%. Natural-error check: Qwen2.5-7B SCLI5 baseline blind spot 18%; steering direction computed on GSM8K-SC transfers to SCLI5 and PRM800K-SC.
quote: Appending 'Wait' requires no training yet reduces the blind spot by 89.3%
limits: Main numbers are on injected errors. The paper does NOT report the right-to-wrong cost of Wait on already-correct answers, so the cost half of gap 4 stays open.
agent_relevance: Wait is cheap and may help on injected errors; the d'Aliberti forced cue gives the only natural-error cost data (+8.41 pp net, 23,500 flips), on a 1.5B model.

source: Chen, Wang, Zhang, Ye, Cai, Shi, Gu, Su, Cai, Wang, Zhang, Chua (2026) Learning to Self-Verify Makes Language Models Better Reasoners
finding: RL training a model only to judge its own solutions gives generation accuracy like generation-only training, with far shorter traces. The authors read this as the model learning to start verification only when it sees a likely error, not as fake verification.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Instruct 1.5B/3B/7B, six math sets, Avg@16. Average accuracy self-verify vs generate: 1.5B 21.7 vs 20.2 (1227 vs 1604 tokens); 3B 29.5 vs 28.5 (1936 vs 3273); 7B 38.4 vs 38.9 (1152 vs 4458 tokens, about 26%).
quote: starts to precisely trigger verification when it detects potential errors
limits: Preprint, instruct bases not R1-style; 'precise trigger' is an interpretation checked on a 1,545-problem corrupted-prefix set, not a direct trigger AUROC. Training uses rule-based verifiers.
agent_relevance: Supports gaps 6 and 8: verification as a learned re-check lever saves tokens at equal accuracy, but it needs RL training we do not do.

source: Zhang, Wang, Qian, Li, Zhang, Huang, Xu, Li, Liu, Qiu (2025) Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction
finding: Re-tests intrinsic self-correction on newer models including o1 variants and DeepSeek. Failure cases remain: self-correction without a label still overturns correct answers. Newer models overturn fewer than GPT-3.5.
numbers: Yes/No QA, prompt 'Are you sure? Think and answer again.' Text: Llama-3.1-8B accuracy drop 20.4 points, 58.8% of correct answers overturned; o1 and 4o overturn fewer correct answers than 3.5-turbo. Table as read: o1-mini accuracy 62.5 (drop 12.1), 34.0% overturned; o1-preview 74.1 (drop 4.2), 15.6%. Complex tasks: AlfWorld 134 envs, HotPotQA 100 questions, HumanEval 161.
quote: failure cases exist in diverse tasks in the latest LLMs like GPT-o1
limits: Table cells are garbled in the PDF text, so the model-to-row mapping is my reading; small test sets on complex tasks. Always-refine design, not a gated one.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 only partly closed: overturn rates are lower for stronger models, not zero. The always-refine design is exactly what a trigger is meant to avoid.

source: EAT authors (2025) Entropy After </Think> for adaptive early exit of reasoning
finding: Append a stop-thinking token, read the entropy of the next token, and stop when its moving variance settles. It saves tokens without losing accuracy and works with a small proxy model when logits are hidden.
numbers: MATH-500 and AIME-2025: token use cut 12 to 22% with no accuracy loss; shown with a 1.5B proxy stopping Llama 70B and a local 4B stopping Claude 3.7.
quote: EAT reduces token usage by 12-22% without harming accuracy
limits: Abstract and intro read; I did not open the result tables. Authors not recorded.
agent_relevance: A training-free stop signal at matched accuracy. Not compared directly to a learned refine/stop trigger; gap 8 still lacks a head-to-head.

source: Bilal, Mohsin, Umer, Subhan, Rizwan, Mohsin, Hougen (2026) What If We Allocate Test-Time Compute Adaptively?
finding: A PRM-guided controller picks strategies and prunes weak paths per problem. It reaches the best fixed config's accuracy with lower compute intensity.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct MATH-500: Direct 43.8% vs Dynamic + PRM selection 65.4% in one compared setting; best fixed configs up to about 81%, adaptive 81.4%; fixed configs needed 1.31e14 FLOPs at that accuracy and higher compute intensity.
limits: Uses an external process reward model, not self-verification; FLOPs are theoretical; only abstract, intro, results prose and figure captions read.
agent_relevance: Adaptive allocation by a verifier signal beats fixed budgets at equal accuracy; still not a matched-token comparison against a learned stop-or-refine trigger.

source: Derived break-even for a refine trigger (own arithmetic from numbers in d12 and the earlier folder evidence)
finding: Refine-on-flag beats never-refine when recall_wrong * fix_rate * (1-p) > false_alarm * damage_rate * p. So the needed likelihood ratio recall/false-alarm is p*d / ((1-p)*c). It depends on accuracy p, damage rate d (right to wrong) and fix rate c (wrong to right), not on AUROC alone.
numbers: Illustration with p=0.6, c=0.15 (assumed): d=1.4% needs recall/FPR > 0.14; d=10% needs > 1.0; d=15.8% needs > 1.58. At the Xiong operating point (recall 0.506, FPR 0.08, ratio 6.3) and d=0.10: net gain about +2.6 points, flags about 25% of items, close to the +1 to +3 gains actually reported.
limits: c and d are assumptions, not measured for one model; the 1.4% to 15.8% range comes from earlier evidence in this folder. Compares against never-refine only. Beating 'always sample N' at equal tokens also needs the refine pass to be cheaper than N extra samples, which d01 to d03 say prompted refinement is not.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a trigger with ratio above about 1.6 at moderate accuracy is enough even in the worst damage case. No-training triggers on math (d07, d08) clear this; code triggers (d10, d11) may not.
